sentences.text: Ceratonykus oculatus is the only known species in the extinct genus Ceratonykus, a theropod dinosaur belonging to the Alvarezsauridae family.
The genus name Ceratonykus means "horned claw" derived from Greek words for horned and claw, while the species name oculatus means "sharp-sighted" or "big-eyed" derived from Latin.
Estimates of its size vary, with one assessment suggesting it was 75 cm long and weighed 760 g, while another study estimated it to be 0.6 meters long and weigh 1 kg.
The skull features a long preorbital region, an ovate upper temporal fenestra, and frontals that are four times longer than wide and narrow wedge-shaped in front view.
Its eyeballs were positioned towards the brain with a diameter of a quarter of the head length, and the optic lobes were displaced towards the anterior, a characteristic shared with extant birds.
The foot structure included tightly adjoining second and fourth metatarsals, with the second metatarsal being shorter than the fourth, alongside considerably reduced third metatarsials.
The species name oculatus, meaning "sharp-sighted," reflects the discovery that its eyes were positioned towards the brain with a diameter of a quarter of the head length.
The optic lobes were displaced towards the anterior, a trait shared with modern birds, which led researchers to propose that the ancestors of alvarezsaurs were likely arboreal.
Despite its distinct features, Ceratonykus has been considered a possible junior synonym of Parvicursor, a debate that continues among paleontologists.
The genus and its only species were named and described in 2009 by Vladimir Alifanov and Rinchen Barsbold, following the discovery of a partial skeleton in 2003.
Preparator Otkhoon Zhargal found the fossil remains of Ceratonykus at the Khermiin Tsav locality in Mongolia within the Barun Goyot Formation.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as MPC no. 100/124, includes an incomplete skull, lower jaw, vertebrae, sternum, coracoids, a humeral fragment, forelimb elements, an ilium fragment, and hindlimbs.
Evidence of an adult individual comes from the fusion of the astragali and tibiae and partially obliterated sutures found in the skeleton.

Alifanov and Savelyev proposed that the ancestors of alvarezsaurs were likely arboreal based on the cerebellum of Ceratonykus, suggesting the complex cerebellum was useful for regulating speed and movement patterns like jumping in terrestrial alvarezsaurs.
The positioning of the eyeballs towards the brain and the displacement of the optic lobes towards the anterior suggest that eyesight was a key sensory system for this animal.

Alifanov and Barsbold originally classified Ceratonykus within the clade Parvicursoridae as the sister taxon to Mononykus, but later studies placed it in the tribe Ceratonykini as the sister taxon to Xixianykus and Albinykus.
The original describers suggested alvarezsaurs were ornithischians rather than theropods, but this hypothesis has not been accepted by the scientific community.
Ceratonykus lived alongside other alvarezsaurids including Khulsanurus, Ondogurvel, and Parvicursor, and it is classified under the parent group Parvicursorinae.

Ceratonykus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, though other sources place it in the Campanian stage spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago, approximately 83 to 71 million years ago in what is now Asia.
The environment where Ceratonykus lived had a semi-arid climate with significant rainfall.

It is debated whether Ceratonykus is a distinct genus or a junior synonym of Parvicursor, with some researchers arguing differences are due to ontogeny or individual variation, while data from the endocranium mold casts doubt on the position of Alvarezsauridae within Theropoda.
